routes.description: Establish the relevant historical data, defend their evidential reliability, and show that divine resurrection explains them more adequately than the principal skeptical alternatives within an independently supported theistic context.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the core data are sufficiently established, the resurrection is not excluded by an improperly fixed prior or evidential threshold, and its comparative explanatory advantages support treating it as the best historical explanation.

motionBridge.description: Connect the established historical data to the conclusion that Jesus's resurrection is their best explanation.

centralBridges.description: Establish the burial, empty tomb, postmortem experiences, and transformed disciple belief as historical data requiring explanation.
Show that fabrication, hallucination, and legendary development lack sufficient explanatory scope or power relative to resurrection.
Justify assessing resurrection within a theistic context in which divine action is not antecedently prohibitive.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Defend best-explanation and probability reasoning as an appropriate form of historical proof without requiring mathematical certainty.
Clarify how cumulative arguments, personal experience, and practical stakes relate to, but do not replace, the historical case.

routes.description: Prevent the resurrection conclusion by challenging the adequacy and reliability of the proposed historical data, defending naturalistic or source-critical alternatives, and requiring evidential support proportionate to the supernatural claim and its asserted divine context.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if uncertainty in the underlying reports, plausible skeptical alternatives, or unresolved prior-probability and evidence-expectation concerns keep resurrection from being warranted as the best explanation.

motionBridge.description: Show that skeptical alternatives and evidential uncertainty prevent the resurrection from being established as the best explanation.

centralBridges.description: Contest whether appearance reports, the empty tomb, and related claims are reliable and sufficiently established historical data.
Preserve sincere error, hallucination, legendary development, or combined naturalistic accounts as live explanatory alternatives.
Show that the resurrection's prior improbability and the expected evidence under divine authorship require more than ordinary-quality historical support.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test whether public counterevidence can override experiential warrant and whether the resurrection claim has a meaningful falsification condition.
Relate the claim's exceptional historical and religious consequence to the degree of evidential caution appropriate before accepting it.

sections.title: Historical Proof, Evidential Standards, and Prior Probability
sections.rationale: This issue governs whether ordinary best-explanation reasoning can establish a supernatural event, how prior probability enters the comparison, and whether a theistic context or the claim's extraordinary character changes the evidential burden.

sections.title: Core Historical Data and Source Reliability
sections.rationale: The comparative inference depends on whether burial, the empty tomb, postmortem experiences, and transformed belief are adequately supported by early and independent sources rather than uncertain or developing reports.

sections.title: Fabrication, Hallucination, and Legendary Development
sections.rationale: This issue tests whether sincere error, grief-related experiences, deliberate invention, legendary growth, or combinations of naturalistic hypotheses can explain the proposed data without invoking resurrection.

sections.title: Experiential Warrant, Falsification, and Practical Stakes
sections.rationale: This issue clarifies the relationship between personal religious experience and public historical evidence, identifies potential defeaters, and determines what role practical consequences may have alongside the historical inference.

chunk-001:c002.proposition: Immediate personal experience of God can rationally ground Christian belief when available evidence is misleading, but belief should yield if the facts genuinely contradict Christianity.

chunk-001:c007.proposition: The resurrection should face the same epistemic standard as other historical claims, while Christianity's potential benefits may provide an additional pragmatic reason for belief without replacing historical justification.

chunk-001:c009.proposition: A low-prior extraordinary event can become probable through ordinary evidence when the evidence is sufficiently more likely on that hypothesis than on its negation.

chunk-002:c002-02.proposition: Resurrection evidence should be assessed within a theistic context established by independent arguments, because a resurrection is not antecedently implausible if a creator God exists.

chunk-002:c002-03.proposition: The crucifixion, burial, empty tomb, postmortem experiences, and transformed disciples are widely accepted historical facts that are best explained by the disciples' resurrection hypothesis under standard explanatory criteria.

chunk-002:c002-06.proposition: Hallucinations lack explanatory power for the disciples' bodily-resurrection belief and lack explanatory scope because they do not account for the publicly inspectable empty tomb.

chunk-002:c002-08.proposition: The core resurrection data, especially the disciples' postmortem experiences, are supported by broad scholarly agreement, very early tradition, and multiple independent attestation rather than late unsupported reports.

chunk-002:c002-10.proposition: Multiple early and independent appearance traditions, including Pauline and pre-Markan material, make wholesale dismissal of the postmortem reports as late legendary development unreasonable.

chunk-001:c003.proposition: Conclusive discovery of Jesus's bones would defeat the resurrection claim and should override otherwise powerful personal religious experience.

chunk-001:c008.proposition: Ordinary-quality historical evidence is inadequate when the claimed resurrection was performed by an omnipotent God who strongly wants people to believe it occurred.

chunk-002:c002-01.proposition: Weaknesses in naturalistic alternatives do not by themselves make resurrection probable because divine intervention carries an extraordinarily low prior probability.

chunk-002:c002-05.proposition: The disciples could have sincerely but mistakenly believed Jesus rose, including through grief-induced hallucinations, so sincere conviction does not establish the resurrection's truth.

chunk-002:c002-07.proposition: Reports of disciple beliefs, group appearances, and post-resurrection events may be unreliable rather than established historical facts requiring explanation.

chunk-002:c002-09.proposition: Increasingly elaborate resurrection appearances in later gospel accounts suggest legendary development rather than stable, independent historical testimony.
